Stated Claim / Post Context:
The Pollycrisis | David Wingrave

Are the feral parakeets taking over the United Kingdom avian friend or foe?

Actual Article Body:

Before we saw a single parakeet, we heard them: a disembodied static that grew louder as we approached Hither Green Cemetery in southeast London. It was an early evening in late June, and we had come to witness an invasion. By the time my friend and I reached the cemetery’s western edge, the clamor was all-encompassing. We hopped the fence and picked our way across the gravestones. Above us now were the birds themselves, their kryptonite-green plumage, scab-red beaks, pearly black collars, and trailing tail feathers unmistakable: Psittacula krameri, the ring-necked parakeet.

Hither Green Cemetery hosts one of the city’s largest roosts. Every day at dusk, a sizable chunk of London’s feral parakeet population returns here, to a specific line of poplars; they like to spend the night in the company of their own kind. We watched them come first in ones and twos, and then in larger chirruping squadrons. Hundreds of them, and then thousands. They swooped in from boroughs unknown to perch briefly in a stand of ornamental cherry trees before making the final flutter into the poplar roost. At maximum capacity, the trees fizzed, erasing the distinction between leaf and feather. Here was a pandemonium, a parakeet concourse. It gave the impression of community, greeting, and conversation. “This,” my friend said, “would make a great cheap first date.”

These birds are not from around here. For the past half century or so, the ring-necked parakeet, an arrival from Asia, has been making itself at home in Britain. In that time the population has become genetically distinct from its forebears, an admixture of two subspecies: P. k. borealis, whose native range spans northeastern Afghanistan and Pakistan, across northern India and Nepal, and east into Bangladesh and Myanmar; and P. k. manillensis, from southern India and Sri Lanka. Of the two, the boreal is the dominant stock, which might help explain why the birds have taken so well to Britain’s cooler, wetter climate. They are not, as their psittacine iridescence suggests, a tropical species, but creatures of the Himalayan foothills.

Most immediately, they are noisy and they are green—so noisy that the novelist Will Self once wrote that, were he to get his hands on one, he would “cheerfully wring its neck”; so green that he busted out a big ole unheimlich to describe their increasing ubiquity. He has a point. Even after seeing these parakeets all my life, the sheer scale of this gathering in an old and oaky English field still felt like encountering a glitch. “Against the light of every season, they seem differently feathered, differently lit,” was how the art critic Isobel Harbison described their strange presence. More straightforwardly, she admired how they were “dressed fabulously.” It’s true. Even the cheerfully avicidal Self admitted they bring a “great gaiety to British skies.” The writer Nick Hunt has perhaps the best line: Flocks of urban parakeets represent a “Ballardian vision,” invoking the science-fiction writer’s altered, mutant futures. If the Hither Green roost does not quite realize the glutinous London of Ballard’s 1962 novel The Drowned World, in which the city has reverted to a primordial mire, it still participates in its spectacle of distorted excess. Thousands upon thousands of bright-green parrots hanging out in drowsy suburban London, a phenomenon every bit as awesome as a salmon run or a migrating swarm of monarch butterflies. For a metropolitan experience of nonhuman life, it is difficult to think of a more impressive display.

As dusk accelerated, the roost began to quiet, and then, in a single moment decided upon only by the parakeets, it fell silent. The day was flown. Time for bed. Now, the poplars fluttered without calls or squawks, only in a low, shuffling susurrus. My friend and I looked at each other, released from the vision. We saw for the first time how the ground had been befouled by their presence. The gravestones, trees, and lawn speckled white with uric paste and cottony down.

For all their splendor, the parakeets are nevertheless a bit of a scandal. Politicians, conservation bodies, land management, and the public have all begun to ask: Do we want tens of thousands of Himalayan parrots squabbling all over our cities? Across their native range, they are known as a significant crop pest. European studies suggest the parakeets have negative impacts on various native bird and bat populations. We know they vector both Newcastle disease, a viral ailment that primarily affects poultry, and Cryptosporidium, a parasite with more general tastes whose characteristic symptom in humans is violent diarrhea. Though plans for a government cull were allegedly considered in 2021, they were abandoned due to potential expense and general impracticality. So parakeet numbers keep climbing and their range keeps expanding. An Oxford researcher estimated that the Greater London population is growing so rapidly that it would need to be cut by 30 percent each year just to keep it stable. A 2014 headline in the Northern Echo (“Who’s a Chilly Boy, Then?”) announced their arrival in Scotland, where Glasgow is now home to the world’s most northerly wild parrots.

Maybe officialdom doesn’t have the stomach for mandated eradication. Maybe its administrative talents are better suited to finding a workaround. As Hither Green Cemetery fell into darkness, central London kept the lights on. Among the corridors and meeting rooms of Whitehall, a change to the law was being discussed. What if the government didn’t have to kill anything after all? What if we could do it ourselves—you and I?

In March of this year, the British government opened a consultation on the quarry list, a catalog of birds that can be shot in season by anyone with a gun and a landowner’s permission. Most of its proposals would remove or restrict the shooting of declining ducks, geese, and waders, but the consultation also invited suggestions for species to add. The British Association for Shooting and Conservation (BASC) duly obliged and put forward twenty-four birds—the ring-necked parakeet among them. Legal provisions for the lethal control of parakeets already exist; as an “invasive nonnative” species, they can, under certain circumstances, be killed without consequence. They appear on two of the government’s “general licenses”: standing permissions, published annually, that landowners and anyone acting on their behalf can utilize without applying or registering, provided the aim is to protect crops or threatened wildlife and that nonlethal methods have proved ineffective or impractical. Quarry status would do away with the need for any such justifications and reorient management away from a defensive posture toward a more general sport-shooting approach. It would allow the public to take matters into its own hands.

How did the ring-necked parakeet become such a common feature of British skies?

How did we get here? How did they get here? How did the ring-necked parakeet become such a common feature of British skies? No one knows. Or not exactly. Origin myths abound: that in 1968 Jimi Hendrix released his pet pair onto Carnaby Street, that in 1951 they escaped from the set of The African Queen, or that in the early sixteenth century they absconded from one of Henry VIII’s royal menageries at Hampton Court. None of these legends stand up to scrutiny: Hendrix’s girlfriend at the time insists the guitarist never owned any parakeets, The African Queen features zero parakeets, and there is no record of parakeets at Hampton Court. Much more credible is the geographic profiling undertaken by Steven Le Comber, an evolutionary biologist at Queen Mary University of London, and his coauthors. The overwhelming likelihood, according to the study, is that the ring-necked parakeet got its start on this island thanks to a steady trickle of runaway pets, deliberate releases, and aviary jailbreaks. This is what those who study invasive species call “propagule pressure”: Successful invasions begin with a lone transplant less frequently than they do with the compounded probability of multiple, sustained introductions. In other words, the likelihood that an introduced organism will become established is somewhat determined by how many chances it is given—and we have given parakeets plenty of chances.

Today, parrot keeping is seen as a somewhat niche activity, but this has not always been the case. Like our planet’s periods of warming and glaciation, the fad for domestic bird keeping has blown hot and cold. The British, who during their age of empire rarely denied themselves an acquisitive impulse, shipped literal boatloads of tropical birds back to the imperial nest in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries. By 1895, London alone sustained 118 wild-animal shops, which fed a parrot fever (metaphor) that was curtailed only by a parrot fever (real): In 1929 and 1930, an outbreak of a parrot-borne bacterial infection called psittacosis caused widespread alarm. The episode generated Britain’s first parrot-panicked headlines: “Parrot Disease,” “Parrot Causes Man’s Death.—Wife in Hospital,” and “Don’t Kiss ‘Polly’!” The resulting 1930 import ban tanked much of the country’s exotic-bird trade, and although there was no legal requirement for owners to dispatch their beloved psittacines, Le Comber has suggested that fear of the disease—before antibiotics, it had a mortality rate of up to 50 percent—might have caused some to release their birds. Such releases are likely responsible for the parakeets observed in Epping Forest in Essex two years later.

London’s avian founding fathers? Not quite. These early, isolated sightings were both ecological and literal dead ends. The Epping parakeets died. So did all the others. Not until Britain’s postwar bird-keeping boom—which between 1947 and 1961 saw the number of pet birds rise from six hundred thousand to eleven million, outnumbering dogs and cats combined—do we find the anonymous progenitors of our current abundance. In every contemporary overhead squawk echoes the creak of a mid-century cage door; in every rapid wingbeat flickers the afterimage of flapping, storm-damaged aviary netting. By 1971, a self-sustaining population had established itself in Croydon. In 1986, Peter Lack’s Atlas of Wintering Birds in Britain and Ireland put the population at about one thousand. The birds soon expanded their range from strongholds in South London and Kent, and estimates in 1997 put the entire UK population around thirty-five hundred. In the early 2000s, a roost on the grounds of the Esher Rugby Club, in southwest London, contained some seven thousand individuals, and its collapse (someone felled the trees for reasons no one can quite agree on) is sometimes held responsible for the parakeets’ subsequent dispersal. The most recent official count throughout the UK, in 2016, put their number at twelve thousand breeding pairs. Today, fifty thousand is commonly cited, though that may be a severe underestimate. If accurate, it would still represent a population increase of 1,567 percent over the last thirty years.

This rapid proliferation has prompted more frequent calls for active parakeet management. Leading the charge to bring the parakeet onto the quarry list has been the BASC. On August 8, two days before the results of the consultation were due to be announced, I spoke to Conor O’Gorman, the organization’s head of policy and campaigns. BASC’s opponents have variously accused them of wanting to hunt parakeets for the hell of it, harboring a xenophobic animus against these very foreign-looking birds, and volunteering too enthusiastically to carry out a private cull. But O’Gorman was keen to emphasize that the proposed change was not about killing for pleasure.

“It’s to give landowners, farmers, an extra flexibility,” he said. “The idea that we as an organization, as the shooting fraternity, want parakeets on the quarry list so we can shoot them for sport is kind of ridiculous.” What BASC wanted, he explained, was to give landowners and farmers a quick legal option when the birds showed up in an orchard or a vineyard. “They’re already on the general license,” he went on, and what that allows for is “trapping. It’s egg pricking. It’s taking youngsters. It’s destroying nests. There’s a whole load of things you can do.” What, then, would quarry status add? Simplicity, O’Gorman said. “Some of those general licenses are about twenty pages long. They were written by lawyers, and if you’re just a normal person like myself, and you want to go out and control a species, well, things can get quite tricky.” He was careful to insist that this was not a cull. “The urban population is here to stay,” he said; quarry status was insurance against potential rural incursions. Get the law in place now, he went on, so that when it comes time to act, people will have legal means to do so.

Frustration that current provisions are caveated and conditioned by pages of legalese handed down from Westminster reflects sharply divergent attitudes toward the birds among Britain’s urban and rural communities. A 2024 study by Alessandro Pirzio-Biroli titled “Not in the Countryside Please!” found that while urban dwellers felt ambivalently about parakeets, negative attitudes rose sharply among respondents in the shires. For somebody who has been petitioning the government for more straightforward means to kill parakeets, O’Gorman seemed to like the birds quite a bit. “They’re lovely,” he said, recalling the first time he saw one, at Windsor Castle many years ago. He was even willing to concede that the antiparakeet brigade might be motivated by prejudice against the exotic. “I can understand the concept,” he said, “that there is this xenophobia underlying the language. That’s something to be conscious of.”

O’Gorman’s candor is disarming, but the solution he advocates would still mean killing thousands of beautiful and increasingly visible birds. His simple certainty that control both is necessary and should take such deadly form is at odds with his obvious fascination with the complexity of the natural world.

The fix O’Gorman endorses may sound drastic, but his precautionary principle is shared by invasion biology, the subdiscipline devoted to the study of species transplanted from their native ranges. There is a long history of organisms moved by humans, whether deliberately or inadvertently, wreaking total havoc upon their new homes. The brown tree snake, native to Indonesia, northern Australia, and Papua New Guinea, was accidentally introduced to Guam by the US military following World War II and promptly ate its way through ten of the island’s twelve endemic forest bird species. Similarly, Nile perch released into Lake Victoria by British colonial forces gulped down roughly two hundred species of homegrown cichlids, fish found nowhere else on Earth. Cane toads in Australia, Miconia trees on Hawaii and Tahiti, rats just about everywhere—the list goes on. And if biodiversity loss, however regrettable, seems like an abstraction in the scheme of things, know that human culture frequently suffers direct impoverishments because of invasives. Chestnut blight, discovered in the United States in 1904 after chestnut trees were imported from Japan, effectively deleted the American chestnut tree from the continent; its products were central to the diet and lifestyles of various indigenous peoples and communities across Appalachia. Phylloxera, an aphid relative, was imported to Europe on American grapevines during the second half of the nineteenth century. The subsequent infestation resulted in the destruction, by some estimates, of 90 percent of all European vineyards.

London’s avian founding fathers? Not quite.

Though the ring-necked parakeet has not yet wrought comparable devastation, the fear remains that it might one day develop the capacity. Invasion biology uses the term lag phase to denote the time between the initial appearance of a nonnative species and its maturation into an invasive scourge. Arrivals initially considered harmless may emerge as significant threats when their population reaches a certain size or as the result of a change in environmental conditions. The Great Britain Non-native Species Secretariat noted in a 2011 risk assessment that parakeets had the potential to be “one of the most destructive bird pests of agriculture.” Their urban concentration has, so far, limited that impact in Britain, but Tim Weston, the director of environment, policy, and politics at the National Gamekeepers’ Organisation, told me that they have already become a threat to cherry blossoms in Kent. “We don’t really have another species that eats flowers,” he said. “And, obviously, if a flock of parakeets descends on your orchard and eats all the blossom, well, you don’t get any fruit.”

And then there are the ecological impacts. Ring-necked parakeets are secondary cavity nesters, which means they raise their young in tree hollows, and unlike primary cavity nesters, such as woodpeckers, they don’t excavate the hollows themselves. This is a common avian strategy employed by a number of British birds, including common starlings, great tits, blue tits, pied flycatchers, common redstarts, stock doves, little owls, tawny owls, Eurasian tree sparrows, and Eurasian nuthatches. Although abundant, the tree hollows favored by these species are not an infinite resource. Evidence from Belgium and Spain suggests that parakeets may outcompete several species, most significantly the Eurasian nuthatch, leading to local declines in areas with large parakeet populations. Greater noctule bats, which also nest in tree hollows, might be at similar risk. If any one of these current nuisances were to become something more ruinous, might we, as O’Gorman pointed out, “look back on these things in twenty or thirty years’ time and say, ‘Oh my God, why didn’t we act?’”

From a curiosity to an established presence—one initially thought to be largely benign—the ring-necked parakeet has been recast as a menace, not just responsible for economic damage and ecological disruption but symbolic of our blighted world and symptomatic of our sclerotic inability to arrest its decline. “Invasive Parakeets Now ‘Unstoppable,’” reported ITV News. “Parakeets Now Outnumber Native British Birds,” warned the Telegraph. “Native British Birds Are So Scared of Invading Parakeets That It’s Putting Them off Their Food,” thundered the Daily Mail, picking up a tradition dating to the psittacosis outbreak nearly one hundred years earlier.

And yet, despite its invasive status, and for all its supposed crimes, the ring-necked parakeet has found plenty of advocates—and invasion biology its fair share of critics. Invasion of the Parakeets, a documentary by the veteran public naturalist Chris Packham that aired on Channel 4 earlier this year, argues that much of the case against them is overblown. Their raids on orchards and vineyards, he indicates, have been confined to a handful of incidents, easily handled. Evidence of their competition for nest holes is inconclusive and, in any case, unlikely to be dramatic. To Packham’s mind, what is driving the panic is something simpler: an underlying fear of newcomers stoked by hysterical press coverage. To remove the birds, he concludes, would be ethically dubious, and—now that they’ve established themselves as part of our everyday environment—its own act of eco-cultural vandalism. Should the efflorescence of parakeets one day bloom into a serious threat to agriculture or the environment, their management ought to be humane and not outsourced to whatever section of the public happens to own suitable firearms.

Flock Together, a bird-watching organization for people of color, is even more explicit in its linkage of antiparakeet sentiment with hostile attitudes toward human arrivals, lamenting that the “bitter cocktail of daily microaggressions and institutional insults” suffered by the parakeet would be “a familiar taste to any British citizen with non-white heritage.”

The ring-necked parakeet has been recast as a menace, not just responsible for economic damage and ecological disruption but symbolic of our blighted world.

Nick Hunt, the author of the 2019 work of “gonzo ornithology” The Parakeeting of London, refuses these broad positions but nevertheless retains a governing affection for the birds. When we spoke, he was in Bristol—in the same spot where, just a few years ago, he recalled hearing a familiar screech and knowing instantly that the parakeets had finally made it to the southwest. It was like the arrival of an old friend, he said. Parakeeting, which grew out of fieldwork conducted from 2015 to 2017, is not even a decade old, but the interim population explosion has already made its framing seem archaic: Hunt and photographer Tim Mitchell go on a quest to, as Hunt puts it, “track down” the birds. Tracking them down today requires merely walking up to the nearest tree and tilting your head back. What prompted the book, Hunt explained, was the feeling that no one was acknowledging their increasingly undeniable ubiquity. “No one was really talking about them, apart from pub rumors. ‘My friend Dave says,’ that kind of thing.”

Things have changed. Since the book’s release, the ring-tailed parakeet has become to many something akin to a civic mascot: vivacious, unashamed, redolent of youthfulness and futurity. When I visited the Kentish Town pub the Parakeet, advertised with a sign that prominently featured the bird, I found it fittingly crammed with annoying yet undeniably vibrant Gen Z kids. Parakeets have been the subject of street murals, featured in fiction (like J. B. Smith’s story “Parakeets of London”), and documented in countless social media posts. Still, for all their cultural visibility, Hunt concedes that we don’t know if a certain quantity might augur a qualitative change in their impact, but to kill the parakeet feels like “punishing success.” He suggests they might offer some consolation, faced as we are with a denuded natural environment: “Everything is about diminishment and decline, but the parakeets are thriving, and they’re doing it in style. It’s a joyous thing to witness. We shouldn’t only be talking about ‘aliens’ and ‘eradication.’ It’s depressing.” His more profound objection is to the underlying rigidity that governs these terms: “Accepting borders and current ranges as the natural way of things, that they can never change, that they must always be fixed in place—well, it seems, paradoxically, to go against the natural order of things.”

Invasion biology has long made use of a troubled vocabulary—terms like exotic, kill on sight, and biological pollution—and wrestled with the ideology that categories such as alien, native, and pristine would seem to confer. Then again, military metaphors applied to rogue organisms are older than the discipline. Darwin himself is often credited with the first usage of the term invasion in an ecological context. In The Voyage of the Beagle, he says of the smothering spread of artichoke thistle across the Uruguayan pampas that he doubts “whether any case is on record of an invasion on so grand a scale of one plant over the aborigines.” It is somewhat surprising, then, given Darwin penned the line nearly two hundred years ago, that invasion biology did not properly coalesce until the early 1980s.

One reason for the delay was that during much of the last three centuries the introduction of nonnative species was not considered a public ill. Domestic rabbits were brought to Australia from England with the first fleet of British settlers in 1788, as both pets and food, although the problems didn’t begin in earnest until 1859, when rangier, cannier wild rabbits were introduced as game. By 1879, they had multiplied to such biblical proportions that farmers were abandoning their properties, the grazing stripped to the last shoot. In a bid to control the plague, cats, ferrets, and mongooses were subsequently introduced. As noted by Daniel Simberloff, a professor of environmental studies at the University of Tennessee and the author of a history of invasion biology, none of these predators successfully reduced rabbit numbers, and several went on to further devastate the native biota.

Sport was a common cause of such disastrous introductions. Brown trout followed the British around the world, feasting on the various smaller fishes they encountered. Nostalgia was another: Notorious imperialist and statue haver Cecil Rhodes is said to have released five species of British songbirds on his Cape Town estate because he missed the sound of an English morning. But aside from the folly of empires, the prime offenders were so-called acclimatization societies. Initially a French phenomenon, the Société Zoologique d’Acclimatation was founded in 1854 and versions modeled upon it soon sprang up in America, Russia, Germany, England, and Australia. These institutions undertook hundreds of introductions, often with some vague pretension to “improve” the local environment: to correct a perceived lack of proper produce or control some pestiferous insect. Some of their initiatives were even more dunderheaded. America, for example, may owe its two hundred million–plus starlings to New York pharmacist Eugene Schieffelin, who as the chairman of the American Acclimatization Society released eighty of them into Central Park (apocryphally as part of a bid to introduce every species mentioned in the works of Shakespeare). None other than Theodore Roosevelt backed the release of hippos into the Louisiana bayou during the brief vogue for “lake cow bacon”: Congressman Robert Broussard proposed importing the animals to control another invasive species, the water hyacinth, and as a source of cheap meat during a national shortage. The plan had support, including from the New York Times and the Washington Post, but House Resolution 23261—the American hippo bill, as it became known—eventually died in committee, possibly because of procedural snags or possibly because it was completely insane. By the early twentieth century, most of the acclimatization societies petered out—or, sometimes, transformed into more modern environmental organizations. Australia’s Acclimatisation Society of Victoria became, for example, Zoos Victoria, which has realized notable conservation successes with endangered bandicoots and frogs.

A series of workshops launched in 1982 by the Scientific Committee on Problems of the Environment gave invasion biology an institutional framework—but a framework is not quite a subject, and the discipline has been debating its own ambiguities ever since. Movement of species is a nebulous concept, given that species have, obviously, always moved around. If we mean movement via humans, do the opportunities provided by climate change count? What’s the baseline? Does the capercaillie—a large bird whose haunting cry was squelched from the forests of Scotland upon its extinction by 1785, before being reintroduced via Swedish stock in 1837—still count as native? Can a species like the Australian dingo, introduced by an unknown, ancient maritime people around four thousand years ago, achieve nativeness? And, to return to Hunt’s point, what does it mean to describe nonhuman species with language akin to that used by some of our most hateful politicians for human migrants?

In 2011, long-simmering arguments within the discipline went mainstream (sort of) when Macalester College professor of biology Mark Davis, along with eighteen signatories, published a paper in the journal Nature titled “Don’t Judge Species on Their Origins,” a plea for invasion biology’s reformation. Davis wrote that the “practical value of the native-versus-alien species dichotomy in conservation is declining, and even becoming counterproductive.” Nativeness, in his view, is a flawed concept and hardly indicative of evolutionary fitness. He pointed out that many introduced species bring substantial benefits and that “the insect currently suspected to be killing more trees than any other in North America is the native mountain pine beetle.” Davis called for an interrogation of the field’s conspicuously militant mindset and concluded that it was “time for conservationists to focus much more on the functions of species, and much less on where they originated.”

Simberloff quickly marshaled a rebuttal against what he saw as a dangerous revisionist position. He and his 141 signatories accused Davis of attacking two straw men: First, most invasion biologists did not “oppose non-native species per se”—only those identified as threats by the Convention on Biological Diversity. Second, they had not ignored the potential benefits of nonnative species; they recognized that many introductions curtail erosion, provide food, and contribute other useful ecological services. “Nobody tries to eradicate wheat,” he pointed out. In addition, Simberloff accused Davis and his allies of downplaying the severe impact of nonnative species. The public, he urged, should remain “vigilant of introductions and continue to support the many successful management efforts.” The battle lines were drawn, and drawn they remain. Today, public, governmental, and institutional approaches tend to side with Simberloff. But a cohort of writers, academics, conservationists, and activists has remained critical of invasion biology’s core doctrines.

The botanist Ken Thompson is one such dissident. His pop science book Where Do Camels Belong? argues that demonizing any species that comes from “somewhere else” is a waste of resources, and that nativeness is a concept fraught with contradiction. In his view, invasion biology has left little room for nuance. Take the zebra mussel, which arrived in North America via ballast water sometime in the 1980s and proceeded to attach itself to any hard surface it could find, clogging pipes, threatening local bivalves, and by one estimate costing the public over $1 billion a year. That sounds bad, but as Thompson writes, for the card-carrying anti-invader, “as far as aliens are concerned, the balance sheet has only a debit column.” He points to the US Army Corps of Engineers’ Zebra Mussel Research Program, which has reported increases in water clarity, aquatic plant abundance, and provision of food for birds and fish, all courtesy of the mussel. Thompson is all for sensible precautions. But the official invasion biologists’ position is, he told me, ideological, not scientific. “It’s not about facts. It’s about their beliefs that aliens are, by their nature, bad.”

Are the parakeets “bad”? It depends on whom you ask. To fruit farmers, they are an emergent pest. To nuthatches, they are a potential nest thief. But to many members of the public, they are a welcome addition to otherwise-gray cityscapes and a spirited reminder—more benign than, say, tick-borne steak allergies—of our changing world. That they readily occupy this ambiguous position is in some ways testament to the weaknesses inherent in invasion biology’s categorical thinking. Its traditionalists have doubled down on blanket labels like native and invader, unable to admit more apt designations like desired or harmful to human interests. Despite the destruction caused by some invasive species, and despite the real need to mitigate their impacts, the notion of a pristine past, free of human influence and its degradations, is an attitude that places us firmly, and ahistorically, outside the nature that invasion biology seeks to preserve. As Thompson notes, an incomplete list of culinary plants introduced to Britain by the Romans would include (deep breath): lentil, medlar, pear, almond, peach, garlic, onion, shallot, leek, cabbage, cucumber, lettuce, turnip, radish, asparagus, rosemary, thyme, basil, walnut, sweet chestnut, grapes, mulberry, and apples that, unlike the native crabapple, are actually nice to eat—most of which your average subject of the crown would defend as traditionally British. Leeks, for example, are the national symbol of Wales.

On August 10, I found myself refreshing a Department for Environment, Food & Rural Affairs webpage for the results of a consultation to amend a forty-five-year-old law “expected 10 August 2026.” When the day came and went, I messaged O’Gorman, the BASC representative, who seemed resigned to governmental delays. “No indication at our end when the outcome will be published,” he wrote back. And so, with the parakeet’s future hanging in the balance, I met up again with the friend who had accompanied me to Hither Green Cemetery. This time, we took a walk through Kensington Gardens, its grass bleached yellow by the summer’s relentless heat waves. Here, on the western bank of the Serpentine, stands a bronze statue of Peter Pan, in the vicinity of which the parakeets are tamer than elsewhere. If you bring an apple, or some nuts, they will even eat from your hand.

Invasion biology has long made use of a troubled vocabulary—terms like exotic, kill on sight, and biological pollution.

“So did you work out if we should kill them all or not?” my friend asked. The parakeets hopped from branch to branch in the surrounding trees, squawking and cocking their heads to see what we had brought them. I said I thought a better question might be “What do we want?” It might not be any easier to answer, but it neither denies the harms wrought by invasive species nor conforms to rigid ecological category. My hope, I said, was to gesture at the inevitability of human intervention and the responsibility it entails. “You’ve become a parakeet centrist,” he replied. Maybe so. Maybe parakeets, with their chirpy evasion of worldly prejudice, are poor candidates for either condemnation or absolution. It is people, not the birds, who must be accountable for their environment. “It’s funny,” my friend said. “I believe all that stuff you just said, but I never really think about them. They’re here now. I can’t really imagine life without them.”

I was reminded of something Hunt told me: When he last visited the Peter Pan statue, he saw a woman watching the parakeets. Eventually, he approached her and learned she was a tourist from the Gulf States. “They’re lovely,” she remarked. “It’s so nice to come here and see them in their natural habitat.”
